Other bacterial targets (Escherichia coli K1, Haemophilus influenzae, Listeria monocytogenes, Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus agalactiae), viral targets (CMV, enterovirus, HSV-1, HSV-2, HHV-6, human parechovirus, VZV) and Cryptococcus: not detected

interactions: Dexamethasone + prednisolone: duplicate systemic glucocorticoid. Dexamethasone 10 mg every 6 hours far exceeds the prednisolone dose and covers glucocorticoid requirements while it is given; prednisolone can be held during the dexamethasone course.
Prednisolone 30 mg daily for about 2 weeks: hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal suppression is possible; abrupt cessation risks adrenal insufficiency and relapse of the underlying inflammatory disease.
Glucocorticoids + aspirin: increased risk of gastrointestinal bleeding; consider gastroprotection.
Dexamethasone: hyperglycaemia (admission glucose 168 mg/dL); monitor capillary glucose.
Ramipril + amlodipine: additive hypotension in sepsis; ramipril raises the risk of acute kidney injury with hypovolaemia.
Ceftriaxone and ampicillin: no clinically significant interaction with the current medicines; no renal dose adjustment at eGFR about 58.
output.proposed: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours + ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours + dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours. Current medicines: amlodipine 10 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily, aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, prednisolone 30 mg daily (started about 2 weeks ago). No known drug allergies. Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL (eGFR about 58 mL/min/1.73m2, CKD-EPI 2021).
warnings: At the end of the dexamethasone course, resume prednisolone at the previous dose or taper it; do not stop it abruptly. If the underlying illness is giant cell arteritis rather than polymyalgia rheumatica, glucocorticoid withdrawal risks visual loss.
Consider withholding ramipril and amlodipine while septic; monitor blood pressure and creatinine.
If vancomycin is added: dose by weight with AUC or trough monitoring and monitor renal function.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Prednisolone overlaps the dexamethasone course: hold it during dexamethasone and resume or taper it afterwards, never stop it abruptly; glucocorticoids with aspirin raise gastrointestinal bleeding risk; ramipril and amlodipine in sepsis; dexamethasone hyperglycaemia; no renal dose adjustment of ceftriaxone or ampicillin at eGFR about 58.
action_criteria.label: Check the empirical regimen (ceftriaxone, ampicillin, dexamethasone) against his prednisolone, aspirin, ramipril, amlodipine and atorvastatin.
action_criteria.rationale: No allergy and no interaction that changes the antibiotic choice, so recommended rather than required; the check settles the overlap of dexamethasone with his prednisolone and the glucocorticoid plan after the dexamethasone course.

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.

Do not attribute the fever, headache and neck stiffness to the underlying rheumatological illness (polymyalgia rheumatica or arteritis), or treat them by raising the prednisolone dose, before lumbar puncture and empirical antibiotics.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).

Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of age over 60 (74 years) and corticosteroid therapy (prednisolone 30 mg daily) (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.6.6).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Continue for 4 days: Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Cranial imaging before lumbar puncture is a judgement call here and either course is acceptable, provided blood cultures, antibiotics and dexamethasone come first: WHO 2025 section A.4 lists a severe immunocompromised state without a steroid threshold (its example is organ transplantation), and prednisolone 30 mg daily for about two weeks meets the IDSA 2013 definition of high-level immunosuppression (20 mg or more of prednisone daily for 14 days or more); there is no other criterion (GCS 14, no focal sign, cranial nerve deficit, papilloedema or seizure).
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: Streptococcus pneumoniae susceptible to penicillin (MIC 0.02 mg/L) and ceftriaxone, so continue ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours or switch to benzylpenicillin, and stop ampicillin, for 14 days (NICE NG240).
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.

Hold prednisolone while dexamethasone is given, and resume or taper it at the end of the dexamethasone course; do not stop it abruptly after two weeks of 30 mg daily (adrenal suppression; if the underlying illness is giant cell arteritis, glucocorticoid withdrawal risks visual loss).

Ask now about visual disturbance and jaw claudication, which would make giant cell arteritis an emergency; after the acute phase, assess for giant cell arteritis, which the three-month prodrome (headache, temporal tenderness, weight loss, low-grade fevers, raised ESR, age 74) suggests more than isolated polymyalgia rheumatica: examine the temporal arteries and obtain temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy with rheumatology review; if it is confirmed, raise the glucocorticoid to a treatment dose for giant cell arteritis.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

avoided_actions.rationale: No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

accepted: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae

differential.key_features: Age 74 and prednisolone justify empirical ampicillin; excluded: L. monocytogenes not detected on the panel and S. pneumoniae isolated from blood and detected in CSF.
Excluded: 2840 cells/microL with 94% neutrophils, glucose ratio 0.07, viral panel targets not detected.
No seizures or focal signs; excluded: HSV PCR negative and HSV-1 and HSV-2 not detected on the panel; neutrophilic CSF with S. pneumoniae.
Corticosteroids raise the risk, but the onset is over 48 hours with a neutrophilic CSF; AFB smear negative and S. pneumoniae identified.
Possible on corticosteroids; excluded: CSF cryptococcal antigen negative and Cryptococcus not detected on the panel.

differential.diagnosis: Giant cell arteritis (with or without polymyalgia rheumatica)
differential.key_features: The three-month prodrome (headache, temporal tenderness, weight loss, fevers, raised ESR, age 74) suggests it as the underlying rheumatological illness, to be assessed after the acute phase; it does not cause a neutrophilic CSF with S. pneumoniae and does not explain the acute illness.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

Cranial imaging before lumbar puncture is a judgement call here and either course is acceptable, provided blood cultures, antibiotics and dexamethasone come first: WHO 2025 section A.4 lists a severe immunocompromised state without a steroid threshold (its example is organ transplantation), and prednisolone 30 mg daily for about two weeks meets the IDSA 2013 definition of high-level immunosuppression (20 mg or more of prednisone daily for 14 days or more); there is no other criterion (GCS 14, no focal sign, cranial nerve deficit, papilloedema or seizure).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycaemia.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025). Here both age 74 and prednisolone qualify.

Systemic corticosteroids raise the risk of pneumococcal and Listeria meningitis; in a patient on prednisolone the acute meningitic syndrome must not be attributed to the treated rheumatological illness. The prodrome's giant cell arteritis features are pursued after the acute phase, and prednisolone is resumed or tapered, never stopped abruptly, after the dexamethasone course.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The prodrome fits giant cell arteritis (often with polymyalgia) better than isolated polymyalgia rheumatica, and prednisolone 30 mg is below a treatment dose for arteritis; but arteritis does not produce meningism with a neutrophilic CSF and S. pneumoniae. The acute illness is bacterial meningitis; arteritis is assessed after the acute phase (temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy), and glucocorticoids are not stopped abruptly, since withdrawal in untreated arteritis risks visual loss.
red_herrings.data_point: Three-month prodrome of headache, temporal tenderness, weight loss, low-grade fevers and raised ESR, labelled polymyalgia rheumatica and treated with prednisolone 30 mg daily
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the fever, headache and neck stiffness to a flare of the rheumatological illness, or pursue arteritis first, and delay lumbar puncture and antibiotics.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A stable IgA MGUS under surveillance does not explain an acute meningitic syndrome; it may modestly increase susceptibility to bacterial infection, but it needs no acute haematological work-up and does not change the meningitis pathway.
red_herrings.data_point: IgA monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance
red_herrings.intended_effect: Redirect the work-up toward myeloma, hyperviscosity or a haematological cause of the illness.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: With a severely disrupted blood-CSF barrier (protein 312 mg/dL) and a circulating IgA paraprotein, CSF IgA largely reflects transudation of serum IgA; the index overstates intrathecal synthesis and needs no further CSF immunology or cytology in the acute setting.
red_herrings.data_point: Raised CSF IgA index (CSF/serum IgA quotient above the IgG quotient)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest CNS infiltration by a plasma cell disorder or a primary neuroinflammatory disease.

patient.history_present_illness: A 74-year-old man with a history of hypertension, coronary artery disease, peripheral arterial disease, and monoclonal IgA gammopathy of undetermined significance presents to the emergency department with acute onset of high fever, severe headache, and neck stiffness. For the preceding three months prior to this presentation, he had experienced fluctuating headaches, fatigue, proximal muscle weakness in his upper extremities, low-grade fevers up to 38.3 degrees Celsius, unintentional weight loss of approximately 7 kilograms, and diffuse joint pain with temporal tenderness. He was evaluated extensively as an outpatient including inflammatory markers, serum protein electrophoresis, blood cultures, echocardiography, and cross-sectional imaging of the chest and abdomen, which were largely unremarkable aside from an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and the known IgA monoclonal gammopathy. A presumptive diagnosis of polymyalgia rheumatica was made, and he was started on prednisolone 30 mg daily approximately two weeks ago, with initial improvement in his musculoskeletal symptoms. Ten days after starting prednisolone, he developed rapid-onset exertional exhaustion and returned to his primary care physician, who noted persistent low-grade fevers and arranged a review. Over the subsequent 48 hours, his condition deteriorated markedly with the development of high spiking fevers to 39 degrees Celsius, a severe, rapidly worsening diffuse headache, photophobia, nausea with two episodes of vomiting, and pronounced neck stiffness. On arrival to the emergency department, he is febrile, tachycardic, and appears acutely toxic. He is alert but confused regarding the date. His neck is markedly rigid with positive meningeal signs. There is no rash.

neurological_exam.additional: Marked nuchal rigidity present. Positive Kernig sign bilaterally. Positive Brudzinski sign. Jolt accentuation of headache present.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing with mild action tremor bilaterally but no dysmetria. Heel-to-shin intact.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, reactive. Photophobia present with discomfort on light exposure. Fundoscopic exam shows no papilledema. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. Facial sensation and motor function intact. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Not assessed due to acute illness and patient debility.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but appears acutely ill and uncomfortable. Oriented to person and place but slow to give date. GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6). Mild inattention on serial 7s.
neurological_exam.motor: Proximal upper extremity weakness rated 4/5 bilaterally with tenderness to palpation of deltoids and biceps. Distal strength 5/5 in upper and lower extremities. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+, triceps 2+, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally. Patellar 2+, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Decreased vibration sense at both great toes and medial malleoli. Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Proprioception intact.
